title: West Syndrome and Epileptic Spasms: Diagnosis and Treatment

steps.title: West Syndrome Triad and Clinical Presentation

vis.alt: Clinical and EEG patterns in pediatric generalized seizures and epileptic spasms
vis.caption: Epileptic spasms manifest in clusters with paroxysmal flexor or extensor contractions (StewardMD).

steps.tx: The diagnosis of **West syndrome classic triad** requires epileptic spasms, hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalography, and neurodevelopmental arrest or regression. Spasms present as sudden flexor, extensor, or lightning mixed contractions that cluster during transitions between sleeping and waking. Prompt recognition prevents delayed therapy and protects neurodevelopment.
steps.say: The classical triad of West syndrome brings together epileptic spasms in clusters, characteristic hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalography, and developmental regression.

steps.title: Infantile Spasms Peak Age of Onset

left.title: Infantile Spasms Window
points: Typical onset between 3 and 8 months of age
Onset beyond 12-18 months termed epileptic spasms

right.title: Diagnostic Pitfalls
points: Frequently mistaken for infantile colic or reflux
Clusters upon waking help clinical suspicion
Normal development halts or regresses rapidly

steps.tx: The characteristic **Peak age of onset** occurs typically between 3 and 8 months of age, with peak presentation at 4-6 months. Spasms occurring after 12 to 18 months are termed epileptic spasms rather than infantile spasms. Caregivers frequently misinterpret these rhythmic flexor jerks as infantile colic, gastroesophageal reflux, or exaggerated startle reflex.
steps.say: Infantile spasms typically begin between three and eight months of age, with peak presentation occurring around four to six months.

steps.title: Hypsarrhythmia EEG Pattern

rows: Loss of normal physiological sleep rhythms

steps.tx: Interictal electroencephalography confirms the classic **Hypsarrhythmia EEG pattern**, characterized by high-voltage chaotic background discharges exceeding 200-300 mcV. Normal cerebral architecture disappears completely, replaced by multifocal epileptiform spikes and slow waves. Ictal recordings during clinical spasms demonstrate generalized electrodecrement with synchronous high-voltage slow-wave bursts.
steps.say: The diagnostic hallmark on interictal electroencephalography is hypsarrhythmia, showing high voltage disorganized activity exceeding two hundred to three hundred microvolts.

steps.title: First-Line Hormonal Protocols
steps.tx: Standard evidence-based **First-line hormonal therapy** utilizes adrenocorticotropic hormone, administering high-dose ACTH at 150 IU/m2/day or low-dose ACTH at 20-30 IU/day for 2 weeks followed by gradual tapering. Oral prednisolone at 4-8 mg/kg/day serves as an effective alternative. Clinicians monitor hypertension, glycosuria, electrolyte shifts, and fatal opportunistic infections during therapy.
steps.say: First line hormonal therapy utilizes either adrenocorticotropic hormone ACTH at high dose or low dose, or high dose oral prednisolone for two weeks followed by a taper.

steps.title: Vigabatrin in Tuberous Sclerosis

vis.alt: Subependymal nodules, cortical tubers, and cellular mTOR dysregulation in tuberous sclerosis
vis.caption: Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules drive infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis complex (StewardMD).

steps.tx: When epileptic spasms develop in children with tuberous sclerosis complex, **Vigabatrin in Tuberous Sclerosis** is the mandatory drug of choice. Oral vigabatrin dosed at 100-150 mg/kg/day achieves complete spasm cessation in over 80% of patients with cortical tubers. Its targeted inhibition of gamma-aminobutyric acid transaminase raises brain GABA concentrations, suppressing subcortical epileptogenic pacemakers.
steps.say: Vigabatrin is the definitive treatment of choice for spasms secondary to tuberous sclerosis complex, achieving spasm cessation in over eighty percent of patients.

steps.title: Vigabatrin Visual Field Toxicity
steps.tx: Prescribing vigabatrin requires strict vigilance for **Vigabatrin visual field toxicity**, an irreversible bilateral concentric peripheral constriction affecting 30-40% of treated infants. Retinal photoreceptor accumulation necessitates electroretinogram or formal perimetry assessment every 3 months during ongoing therapy. Once clinical and electrographic remission is maintained for six months, therapy is safely tapered to mitigate permanent vision loss.
steps.say: Permanent bilateral visual field constriction occurs in thirty to forty percent of children on vigabatrin, demanding baseline and serial electroretinography every three months.

steps.title: Early Cessation Predicts Outcome

rows: Profound cognitive impairment and intractable epilepsy

steps.tx: Data from the International Collaborative Infantile Spasms Study demonstrates that **Early cessation predicts outcome**, where complete resolution of clinical spasms and disappearance of hypsarrhythmia within 14 days of starting treatment independently predicts preserved neurodevelopment. Delayed presentation or refractory ongoing discharges compounds severe global intellectual disability and motor handicap.
steps.say: Prompt electroclinical response within fourteen days of initiating therapy is the single strongest determinant of long-term neurocognitive outcome.

steps.title: Evolution to Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome
steps.tx: Long-term longitudinal follow-up reveals **Progression to Lennox-Gastaut** syndrome occurring in approximately 20-50% of children with refractory infantile spasms. As neural networks mature, the chaotic hypsarrhythmic background evolves into generalized slow spike-and-wave discharges at 1.5 to 2.5 Hz, accompanied by drug-resistant atonic drop attacks, atypical absences, and nocturnal tonic seizures.
steps.say: Twenty to fifty percent of children with refractory infantile spasms eventually progress to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome with polymorphic intractable seizures.
